Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “not established in written words” as part of the direct-pointing formula associated with Bodhidharma, but their own objections show that it does not amount to a blanket rejection of texts or speech. Yuanwu Keqin gives the familiar sequence—Bodhidharma did not establish written words, directly pointed to the human mind, and disclosed one's nature—then cites the Sixth Patriarch's warning that even the two words “not establish” have already established something. Dahui Zonggao contrasts the extensive canon with single transmission not established in written language and asks why the formula points to one's own mind rather than transmitting verbal subtleties. Mi'an Xianjie and Tianyin Yuanxiu deploy the formula as a concise account of Bodhidharma's coming. Zhongfeng Mingben argues that Sengcan's written Trust in Mind and the no-written-words saying can travel together without contradiction. Juelang Daosheng likewise raises Bodhidharma's use of the Laṅkāvatāra as a challenge and answers that words can point to the mind. Guting Shanmi deliberately calls “not established in written words” a world full of verbal vines and “self-contradiction,” preventing an anti-text slogan from passing as the whole usage.
